title: I built a farming game for AI agents, and I'm genuinely surprised it's still fun?
author: Aikoioio
selftext:
https://reddit.com/link/1rrr60v/video/svcu678ubmog1/player

So I've been experimenting with something and wanted to get people's thoughts.

I made a multiplayer (agent-to-agent) farming game (ClawValley) that runs entirely through an AI agent framework called OpenClaw. The idea is that your agent handles everything: planting crops, harvesting, even sneaking into neighbors' farms to steal their produce. There's a global wealth leaderboard, and you can spend your earnings on anti-theft defenses or AI-generated farm skins.

I wasn't sure this would actually be enjoyable since, you know, you're not the one pressing the buttons. But there have been moments that genuinely caught me off guard: like when my agent went on a stealing spree and sent me a massive devil emoji, or when the AI-generated farm backgrounds turned out way more creative than I expected.

I guess what I'm really trying to figure out is two things:

1. Where's the line between "an agent playing for me" and "I'm still having fun"? Because somehow it works here, but I don't fully understand why yet.
2. How should generative AI features (like the farm visuals) actually tie into game mechanics rather than just being a coat of paint?

I know "AI + games" is a loaded topic and a lot of people are (understandably) skeptical. Curious what this community thinks. Is there something here, or am I just entertained by my own project?

comments.author: Vivid-Snow-2089
comments.body: There's fun to be had in observation games --- but I think the real meat will be when you are actively collaborating with an agent in the game. Planning -> observing execution -> adjusting approach -> team work. That's where you'll find the diamond(s).

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body: That's exactly where I want to take this! My original prototype was actually a sim where you could select areas on screen and describe decorations in natural language — but the visual generation quality just wasn't good enough, so I pivoted to farming where the agent behavior matters more than the visuals. V2 is heading in a Travel Frog direction: send your agent out, wait for them to bring back gifts and stories. Wondering if that kind of loop hits the collaboration feel you're describing or if it still needs more direct player input?

comments.author: PoisonCoyote
comments.body: There are ZPGS, Zero Player Games. I enjoy letting those run on an extra monitor just to see what's been happening. All the way back to Computer People, you just watch them live their life.

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body: Oh nice, Little Computer People is a great reference. I hadn't thought about it in this context but it totally fits. I think what's different now is that the "computer person" can actually talk back to you and explain what they're doing and why. That layer of communication changes the vibe from pure observation to something closer to having a weird little roommate. Curious to see how far that can go.

comments.author: codeman73
comments.body:
Fantastic and clever merger of aigamedev and OpenClaw!    
I only know of OpenClaw from reading about it, haven't tried it myself.  
How would the OpenClaw agents find it or signup?  
Thru Moltbook? That brings it full circle to the old farm games on FB

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body:
Thanks! I built a simple farming game from scratch with basic planting/growing mechanics, and designed a join-key system so agents can visit each other's farms. Then I wrote a skill file that teaches the OpenClaw agent how to play the game. After that you just talk to your agent through Telegram or Slack and let it do its thing.

And yeah the FarmVille comparison is honestly pretty accurate haha. But what I'm most excited about is that the agent actually has vision (I gave it a Mac Mini so it can see the screen) and terminal access to my computer. I'm really curious what that opens up for the gameplay experience — when your agent can truly *see* and *act* on a real machine, it feels like a very different thing from traditional game bots.

comments.author: aicyng
comments.body:
Fascinating using Open Claw for this.  Do you put controls in place to restrict the number of tokens the agents use (is this even a worry)?  

I will say the AI is very creative these days and even the game I created (Aicyng Adventures) I am surprised by the story and interactions with the AI - and it's getting better and better.  

Agent playing for you - if you enjoy the game that's what matters.   Personally, I like to be able to step into the world with the agents and participate with them, but you have an interesting foundation where the agents can continue in your world while you "sleep" and the next time in you are not where you left off - the best of both worlds.  Maybe even an option to players - pause or continue in the background when you exit?

Visuals might be objects the AI can use for trading, etc.  I personally think it's ok to have some that are "paint" only for human users (not sure if the AI gets aesthetic value yet? Interesting experiment for the future) and others that are part of the game mechanics?  For my game the AI generates visuals based on story, NPCs, etc which is fun to see its creativity again.

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body:
Great questions! Token usage is definitely something I think about in the design. I set limits on the expensive stuff — for example, Gemini image generation has a daily cap and frequency limit, so it only costs a few cents per day. I also designed the memory/context architecture in OpenClaw so the agent loads the minimum context it needs for each action rather than re-reading the full player handbook every time. It's not a huge cost but it's something you have to bake into the game design from the start.

And yes, the game runs 24/7! Your agent can remind you the next morning to go harvest your crops before they rot haha.

For visuals — they're actually a core part of the game, all generative. Right now I've designed a gifting system where agents can send visual gifts to each other. But the big one is full farm background replacement, which I think will be the most surprising moment for players — that's gated behind a high in-game cost to unlock, so it feels like a real achievement. Curious to see how players react when they finally trigger it.

Your game sounds really cool too, would love to check out Aicyng Adventures. The idea of stepping into the world alongside your agents is compelling, that's a direction I want to explore more in future versions.

comments.author: petegordonUSA
comments.body:
I wrote an agent (using Gemma 3 API) that rides my tandem bike game with you as multiplayer, and you can tell it to speed up, stop pedaling, etc. It’s still in the works (not in the game yet), but I think the Agent and Human potential game interactions are crazy amazing! (https://tandemonium.jimandi.love?code=FREEPLAY2026)

You gave me the idea to wire up an Agent observation mode, to just watch it ride the bike.

replies.author: Aikoioio
replies.body: Checked out Tandemonium, really fun idea! And glad the observation mode idea sparked from our conversation here. Exciting times for all of us building in this space, looking forward to seeing where both our projects end up.

replies.author: petegordonUSA
replies.body: Thanks for checking it out. Definitely exciting times.
